Off draws the same rows in the same order, without the headings, their counts and their group menus.
Draw the month as a calendar
Off reads the month as the week does — a heading per day that has anything on it, and the rows under it.
Where the calendar is cut into rows, and how the week span is grouped.
An entry held at an hour is announced ahead of it; a day with dated entries and deadlines is announced once, in a digest.
How long before its hour. A deadline with a date of its own is not announced here — it reaches the digest through the warning window it already carries.
And again at the hour itself
Two notifications about the same entry: one ahead of it, one when it starts.
One notification naming what the day holds: entries without an hour, deadlines inside their warning window, and how much is overdue.
Notifications are refused, so nothing would be seen.
Exact alarms are not allowed: a timed entry would be announced within the hour rather than at the minute.
One notification per entry, ahead of its hour by the lead time chosen in the settings.
One notification a day naming what it holds: dated entries without an hour, deadlines and arrears.
Shown for a moment while an entry closed from a reminder is written to the notes.
This build carries no licence list. It is written by tools/licenses.sh and by the build itself; a build that skipped both has nothing to show here.
Fetch from the server, then hand it what was committed here. Nothing is merged: notes that moved on both sides are reported rather than resolved.
No collection has a server yet. The notes are kept on this device until one is given an address in the settings.
The collections, the directory each of them reads and the server it syncs with.

Writes a task into the file the collection receives new ones in; the file and which end of it is used are named in the settings. The keyword, the priority and the date are chosen on the screen it opens.

Opens whatever the phone recognises speech with and writes what was said as a task straight away, with no screen in between: "call the doctor tomorrow at 15:00" is read by the same rules a typed phrase is. A line at the foot offers to take the entry back. The language is the one the phone is set to; both grammars are read either way.
One span back: a day, a week or a month, whichever is on screen. The plan can also be dragged sideways by its heading.
One span forward: a day, a week or a month, whichever is on screen. The plan can also be dragged sideways by its heading.
Back to the day being lived through.
Two ways to read the same day: the hours it spans, with each entry against its own time, or every entry as a line ordered by date.
How much of the plan to read at once: today, the week around it, the whole month, or every task still open — dated or not. The hour axis draws a day, so the wider spans are shown as the list.

Narrows the agenda to the notes a tag takes, by the name of the file each entry came from. The tags are declared by the notes themselves, in .markdown-org/tags.json, and travel with them — the editor extension reads the same ones. Which collections are read is a separate choice, made by the chips below.
%1$s reads %2$s. Press to take its entries off the agenda and back.
What the sync just attempted did. A run over several collections ends with the answer of the last one, and the lines below name each of them.
Commits made on this device that the server has not been given. They stay counted until a sync gets them across, and nothing is lost meanwhile.
When the notes on screen last matched the server. A failed attempt leaves this as it was — it says how old the notes are, not how the attempt went.
What the walk over the notes ran into. The entries it did find are on the agenda below; this says what is missing from it.
Act on every entry of “%1$s” at once, in one commit that can be put back.
Date every entry of the band today. A missed repeat is caught up to its next occurrence instead, keeping its repeater.
Take the planning date off every entry of the band. The tasks stay, and leave the agenda until they are dated again.
Mark every entry of the band cancelled, writing the keyword into the note it came from.
Opens the heading\'s own text and the lines under it. The keyword, the priority and the dates are left to the actions above; the edit is written to the file and committed like any other.

Carries the heading and everything under it into the main file of this collection, and takes it out of the file it is in now. The text travels unchanged; where it lands is what the collection\'s settings say.
Opens the markdown files of this collection to choose from. The move is the same one: the whole entry, into the file you name.
Offers the whole note to a markdown editor of your choosing. What it writes is committed here by the next sync, under a message nobody chose; until then the edit is on this device alone.
The file the task is written in and the line its heading is on, inside the directory of its collection.
Writes DONE into the heading and commits. The task leaves the agenda and stays in the note.
Moves every dated line that carries a repeater on to its next occurrence after today, and sets the keyword back to TODO. Nothing is closed: the task returns on its new date.
Writes CANCELLED into the heading. A note that already spells it CANCELED keeps that spelling.
Writes TODO into the heading, whatever it carried before.

"move it to friday at 16:00 and make it urgent" — reads the keyword, the date, the hour, the repeater and the priority out of the sentence and writes all of them into this entry at once. A phrase can also empty a field: "no date", "remove the time", "no repeat". A word the rules do not understand changes nothing at all, and is named instead.

Opens whatever the phone recognises speech with and adds what it heard to the field, without changing the entry — press Apply when the sentence reads right. The language is the one the phone is set to; both grammars are read either way.
The [#A] cookie of the heading. A, B and C are what org-mode uses out of the box, and the level in force is drawn as the selection; another one appears here when the note carries it.
Moves the date of the planning line by one day. The time, the repeater and the warning cookie stay as written, and the weekday is rewritten to match in the language the file uses.
Writes the day chosen in the calendar into the planning line the task already has, or takes that line out of the note. The time, the repeater and the warning cookie stay as written.
Writes a planning line the task does not have yet, on the day chosen in the calendar. Spelled the way the file spells its other dates: the same weekday language, and the same framing.

Writes the hour into the timestamp the planning line already carries, or takes the hour off and leaves the day. The date, the repeater and the warning cookie stay as written, and an entry with no hour is drawn above the clock rather than at one.
Writes a separate entry at the new time, naming the occurrence it stands in for. The series is left exactly as it is, and this day shows the new entry instead of the one the series would have had.
Adds this day to the list of occurrences the series does not have. The series goes on repeating, and this one day is left out of it.
Which collection every field below is about. The agenda reads all of them at once; this only says which one is being edited.
Another directory of notes, with its own address and its own token. It is added empty and starts being read once it is saved.
Stops the screen asking for an address. The notes stay in the directory below, and a server can be given later without them going anywhere.
Deletes the stored token when the form is saved. A private repository stops syncing until another one is entered.
The private key, its passphrase and the fingerprint of the server. Only an ssh:// address uses any of it.
Deletes the stored private key when the form is saved.
Makes an ed25519 key on this device and keeps the private key here. The public key appears below, for pasting into the server.
Puts the public key on the clipboard. It is of no use on the phone: the server is where it goes.
Opens, in the browser of this device, the page of the host above where tokens are issued. A host this application does not know the pages of opens at its front page.
Opens, in the browser of this device, the page of the host above where public keys are added. Copy the key first: pasting it is what the page is for.
Fills the field above from the system picker. What is stored is a path either way — the notes are read by path, not through the picker.
Opens the screen of the platform where access to all files is granted. A directory outside the application\'s own storage cannot be read without it.
Takes this collection off the agenda and forgets its address, branch and token. The directory and every note in it stay on the device.
The headings say what a row is — scheduled for the day, without an hour, or how long ago it slipped — and carry the actions over a whole band. Turning them off gives their height to the rows.

The phone answers this by default, from its own language and region. State it here when the habit and the phone disagree: the answer decides which day heads the calendar\'s first column and which seven days a week span covers. Changing it asks for the agenda again.

A calendar says how the month is shaped: which weeks are full, where the arrears sit, which stretch is free. A day is opened to read what is actually on it. The list says what is in the month and takes a scroll to say it.

Nothing is announced while this is off, and no alarm is held. What is announced is decided from the same agenda the screen draws, so an entry closed on another device stops being announced as soon as the notes are fetched.

The lead time is the same for every entry: the notes say nothing about how long it takes to get anywhere, and a lead time per entry would have to be written into them. "At the moment" is a lead time of zero rather than the absence of a reminder.
For an entry worth being told about twice — the notice ahead of it to get ready, and the one at the hour to start. With a lead time of "at the moment" the two coincide and only one is raised.
An entry with a date and no hour has no moment to announce, so the day is announced instead — once, at this hour, whatever it holds. What it says is read when it fires, not when it is planned.
Opens the screen of the platform where notifications from this application are allowed. Without it the plan still stands and fires, and nothing of it reaches the screen.
Opens the screen of the platform where exact alarms are allowed. Without it the platform delivers an alarm within an hour of its time, which for a meeting is not a reminder.
What the application carries besides its own sources, and under what terms.
What was left by the run that stopped unexpectedly. It is worth attaching to a report; nothing is sent anywhere by itself.
Which build is installed. Two builds of the same version differ only by the commit, which is why it is here.
Writes the fields into the settings of this collection. The notes are read again straight away, and the server is only contacted by a sync.
Leaves the form without writing anything. What was typed is lost; what was stored stays.

The collection chosen here is the one every field below belongs to. An address or a token typed while the wrong chip is picked is written into that other collection, and the mistake is only seen at the next sync.

Notes kept at home and notes kept for work are two collections. The agenda draws both together, each row marked with a colour of its own; the form is switched between them by the chips, and the token of one is never sent to the host of the other.

A local collection is fetched from nowhere and pushed nowhere: the notes are the files on this device and no more. What is written here does not reach another device, and a phone that is lost takes them with it.

A first launch with no repository ready: the notes stay in the directory below and the agenda works as it does. An address is filled in a week later, and the files already there become the first commit.
The repository this collection is fetched from and pushed to — an https:// or ssh:// address, or the path of a repository on this device. An empty field keeps the notes here and sends them nowhere.

The address decides which credential is used: https:// is authenticated by the access token below, ssh:// by the private key. Changing it moves nothing — the directory of notes stays as it is, and the next sync is against the new server.

https://gitlab.com/user/notes.git fetches over https and asks for a token. ssh://git@gitlab.com/user/notes.git uses the key of this device instead, and asks for nothing once its public key is on the server.
Which branch of the repository is read and written. An empty field follows whatever the server calls its default.

The notes are only ever fast-forwarded: a branch that has moved on the server and on the phone at once is not merged here, and the sync stops with a notice instead. A branch of the phone\'s own keeps two devices out of the same commits.
A repository whose default is main needs nothing here. A phone set to notes-phone writes into that branch alone, and the laptop merges it into main whenever it likes.

What an https:// address is authenticated by: a personal access token issued by the host, not the password of the account. A stored token is never shown again, and an empty field keeps the one that is stored.

Without one, a private repository is neither fetched nor pushed. The token also carries what is allowed: one issued for reading alone fetches the notes and fails at the first push, which arrives as a sync error rather than as a word about permissions.

On GitLab the token is made under Settings → Access Tokens with the scope write_repository; on GitHub it is a fine-grained token with Contents set to read and write. The button under the field opens that page for the host the address names.
The private key an ssh:// address is authenticated by, in OpenSSH format. It is kept on this device and never leaves it. A key made by the button below fills this in by itself.

An ssh:// address uses the key and never looks at the token above. Nothing is fetched until the public key is added to the account on the server: the server refuses the connection, and the sync reports it as a failed authentication.

The key is created here, its public key copied and pasted into GitLab under Settings → SSH Keys, and the address written as ssh://git@gitlab.com/user/notes.git. Nothing is asked at sync time after that.
The passphrase of the private key above, for a key that was created with one. A key made on this device has none, and the field stays empty.

An encrypted key cannot be read without it, and a sync that cannot read the key fails with an authentication error rather than asking for anything. What is typed here is kept on this device beside the key itself.
A key made on a laptop by ssh-keygen under a passphrase and pasted into the field above needs that passphrase typed here once. A key made by the button below is stored unencrypted and needs nothing.

The public key is what the server is told to trust, and it is added on the server rather than here. Until it is, an ssh:// address is refused at the first sync: a key that exists only on the phone means nothing to the host.

The key is copied, the page of the host is opened by the button beside it, and the line is pasted into GitLab under Settings → SSH Keys. The fingerprint shown under the key is the server\'s own, remembered at the first connection and compared at every one after it.
The directory whose markdown files this collection reads and writes. An empty field means the application\'s own storage, which no other application on the phone can open.

Every markdown file under this directory joins the agenda, so a directory holding the whole of Documents is read slowly and shows entries that were never meant for it. A directory outside the application\'s own storage is also unreadable until access to all files is granted below.

/storage/emulated/0/Documents/notes holds the files a laptop syncs by git as well, and a cable reaches them without this application. A directory under Downloads works too — together with every markdown file that happens to be in it.

Android hands an application its own storage and nothing else. Without this permission a directory chosen anywhere else is read as empty: the agenda shows nothing and reports no error, because from where it stands there is nothing to report.
The notes are kept in Documents/notes so a computer can reach them over a cable. The permission is granted once, on the screen of the platform, and the agenda fills the next time the notes are read.

Everything written from the agenda — typed, dictated or said as a phrase — goes into this one file, so what was captured on the phone is found in one place rather than spread over the notes. A file that does not exist yet is created at the first task.
inbox.md takes what is captured during the day. In the evening the entries are moved into the files they belong to from the sheet of the task, which offers the main file named below.
Whether a new entry is written at the top of the file or added at its end. Read by a task made here and by an entry moved into another file.

At the start is what is read first the next morning, without scrolling. At the end is what two devices writing into one file can both do: two additions at the end of a file come together without hand-sorting far more often than two at its top — where branches are merged at all, on a computer.

A phone capturing a dozen tasks a day into inbox.md writes at the start and reads them from the top. A file a laptop appends to as well is set to the end, and the additions of both land under one another.

Without a main file, an entry moved out of the file for new tasks has its target typed by hand every time. Named here, that file is what the sheet of a task offers first, and the usual move costs one press.
New tasks land in inbox.md while the main file is tasks.md: an entry captured in the morning is moved into tasks.md from its sheet, and the file for new tasks stays short enough to read.

A day holding a meeting at 10:00, two tasks with no hour and one overdue since Monday: grouped, it reads as three headings with their counts and their menus; ungrouped, as four rows in the same order, with the height of the headings given back to them.

A month planned unevenly: the calendar shows at a glance that the second week is full and the third is empty, and a day is tapped to read what is on it. The list says the same in headings, one for every day that holds anything, and takes a scroll to say it.

A meeting at 15:00 with an hour of lead time is announced at 14:00, and the digest at 09:00 names what the day holds without an hour. With this off, both stay in the notes and neither reaches the screen.
An hour before a meeting at 15:00 is a notification at 14:00 — time to leave. Five minutes suits a call taken where one is sitting already, and "At the moment" announces it at 15:00 itself.
A meeting at 15:00 with an hour of lead time: one notification at 14:00 to get ready and another at 15:00 to start. With this off, only the one at 14:00 is raised.

The digest at 09:00 says the day holds three entries without an hour, one deadline inside its warning window and two entries overdue. The meeting at 15:00 is not in it: an entry with an hour is announced ahead of that hour, by itself.

The trace names the place the run stopped in, which is the whole of what makes a report worth acting on. It stays on the device until the button under it forgets it, and nothing of it is sent anywhere by itself.

The application closes while a month is being drawn. The trace is copied from here into an issue at the project page, together with the version and the commit from the line at the foot of this screen.
What the component is, the licence it is under and what in this application uses it. Press to read the full text.
Say what to change about this entry
Open the note in another app
The keyword, the priority and the dates are written by the actions of the sheet, not typed here.
The text under this heading is too long to edit here; open the note in another app.
The heading as the file has it, markup included. The keyword and the priority cookie are not part of it: a title that reads as one is refused rather than written.
What stands under the heading, up to the next one. The planning lines are not part of it, and a line that reads as one is refused.
Leaves the entry as the file has it. Nothing typed here is written until Save.
Writes the heading and the lines under it back into the note, in one write and one commit. An entry saved unchanged leaves the file byte for byte as it was.
Say the task in one phrase
This phone has nothing to recognise speech with — type the phrase instead.
The phrase was not understood in full, and nothing was changed
The phrase named nothing to change

"call the doctor tomorrow at 15:00, every week" — reads a date, an hour, a repeater and a priority out of the sentence and fills the fields below with them; whatever the rules do not understand is added to the heading. Nothing is written to the notes — the fields are yours to correct first. A second phrase refines what the first left: "at 16:00" moves the hour and keeps everything else.
What the task says. The keyword, the priority and the date are chosen below and written around it.
The lines that go under the heading. Optional: a task is a heading, and the text under it is what it needs explaining.

Opens whatever the phone recognises speech with and adds what it heard to the field, without touching the fields below — press Fill in when the sentence reads right. The language is the one the phone is set to; both grammars are read either way.
Leaves without writing anything. Nothing reaches the notes until Create.

Writes the task into the collection\'s file for new tasks and commits — at the start or at the end, as the collection is set. Unavailable while the heading is empty: the core refuses to write a heading that says nothing.
Which set of notes takes the task. The file it is written into is the file for new tasks of that collection, named at the foot of the screen.

The word the heading starts with. TODO is what the agenda plans for; DONE and CANCELLED write a task already closed; without one the heading is a note, shown where its date falls. The words are the format and stay as they are in every language.

The [#A] cookie of the heading. A, B and C are what org-mode uses out of the box, and a new task carries none unless it is said otherwise; the sheet of the task offers the rest of the scale once it is in the notes.

Which planning line is written: SCHEDULED for the day the work starts, DEADLINE for the day it is due. Without a chosen day no planning line is written at all, and the task shows up in the flat list of tasks rather than on a date.
+1w steps once from the date written; ++1w steps until it passes today; .+1w counts from the day it was done. The unit is d, w, m, y or wd for working days.
Not a repeater: those are written +1d, ++2w, .+1m, +1wd

The hour the entry is held at, written into the timestamp after the day. Without one the entry takes the whole day and the agenda draws it above the hours. Offered once a day has been chosen: there is no hour to be held at on a task that is not planned for a day.

What makes the date a series rather than one occurrence. The ready answers are written ++1d, ++1w, ++1m and ++1y: completing an overdue task moves it to the next occurrence ahead of today rather than one step from the date in the file. Every… takes any repeater the format has.
No application on this device opens markdown files.
The task could not be changed
The file has changed; sync and try again
The task has no date to move
This repeater cannot be advanced here yet
The file is no longer there
The file is not UTF-8; convert it and try again
The file name is not UTF-8, so the task cannot be changed
The collection this task came from is no longer set up
Another collection is already that directory
The directory is inside another collection, so its notes would be read twice
what the chip on the agenda says
The agenda stops showing its notes. The directory and everything in it stays on the device; the address, the branch and the token of this collection are forgotten.
Saved, but not committed; the next edit or sync will commit it
The task limit was reached; the list is incomplete
The reason is in the log
